Prophesieth
prŏf'e-sī-eth
v. (third person singular of prophesy: to speak forth the word of God; rendering Hebrew naba' and Greek propheteuo)
Greek propheteuo, from pro-, forth or before, and phemi, to speak — to speak forth. The prophet is first a mouth for God and only secondarily a foreteller.

Biblical Definition

Jeremiah gives the test that governs the office: “The prophet which prophesieth of peace, when the word of the prophet shall come to pass, then shall the prophet be known, that the LORD hath truly sent him” (Jer 28:9). A prophecy of peace is the easy word, the popular word, and the one Hananiah had just given; the burden of proof lies on the comfortable prophet, and time is the examiner. Ezekiel meets the opposite evasion: the house of Israel says “the vision that he seeth is for many days to come, and he prophesieth of the times that are far off” (Eze 12:27) — conceding that the word is true while pushing its fulfilment beyond the reach of repentance. Zechariah records the day when a father and mother would themselves execute a lying prophet from their own house (Zec 13:3). In the New Testament the word turns pastoral: “he that prophesieth speaketh unto men to edification, and exhortation, and comfort” (1Co 14:3), and prophesying is preferred above tongues precisely because it builds the church rather than the speaker: “he that prophesieth edifieth the church” (1Co 14:4). The canon being closed, the dictionary holds the cessationist position: what remains is the ministry that Corinthians describes — the church built up by the plain declaration of God's already-given word.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to prophesy as to foretell future events; to predict; and, in Scripture use, to utter predictions and to preach; to instruct in religious doctrine.

expand to see more

PROPHESY, v.t. To foretell future events; to predict.

2. To foreshow.

PROPHESY, v.i. To utter predictions; to make declaration of events to come. In Scripture, to preach; to instruct in religious doctrine; to interpret or explain Scripture or religious subjects.

Key Scripture

Jer 28:9 — "The prophet which prophesieth of peace, when the word of the prophet shall come to pass, then shall the prophet be known, that the LORD hath truly sent him."

Eze 12:27 — "Son of man, behold, they of the house of Israel say, The vision that he seeth is for many days to come, and he prophesieth of the times that are far off."

1Co 14:3 — "But he that prophesieth speaketh unto men to edification, and exhortation, and comfort."

Modern Corruption

The modern prophetic movement has restored the title without the test: men prophesy of peace and prosperity, and Jeremiah's standard of fulfilment is never applied to a word that fails.

expand to see more

Jeremiah 28 is the chapter the contemporary prophetic movement has to answer, and it is short enough to read in a minute. Hananiah prophesied peace — within two full years the vessels return, the king comes home — and he did it in the name of the LORD of hosts, publicly, in the house of the LORD, before all the people. Jeremiah's reply is the rule of verse 9: the prophet of peace is proved by fulfilment, and Deuteronomy 18:22 had already fixed the penalty for failure. Hananiah died that same year. The New Apostolic Reformation and the broader charismatic prophetic industry have restored the title, the platform, and the confident announcement of coming peace and prosperity, and have quietly retired the test. Failed words are re-dated, spiritualised, or blamed on the hearers' unbelief; the man who gave them keeps his conference schedule. The dictionary is cessationist and holds that the canon is closed, but the point here is one that even a consistent continuationist must feel: a movement that will not apply Deuteronomy 18 and Jeremiah 28 to its own prophets has not restored the office — it has abolished the only safeguard the office ever had. Meanwhile 1 Corinthians 14:3 stands, and its criterion is not spectacle but whether the church was built.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew naba' (H5012), to prophesy, to speak by inspiration; nabiy' (H5030), a prophet, a spokesman; Greek propheteuo (G4395), to speak forth God's word.

expand to see more

Hebrew naba' (H5012) — to prophesy, to speak or sing by the Spirit; used of Saul among the prophets and of Ezekiel commanded to prophesy to the bones; Ezekiel 37:4, 1 Samuel 10:11.

Hebrew nabiy' (H5030) — a prophet, a spokesman for another; Aaron is Moses' nabiy', which defines the office exactly; Exodus 7:1, Deuteronomy 18:18.

Greek propheteuo (G4395) — to speak forth the mind of God; in the epistles a gift of edification, exhortation and comfort to the assembly; 1 Corinthians 14:3-4, 14:31.

Usage

"“The prophet which prophesieth of peace…then shall the prophet be known” — the burden of proof on the comfortable word."

"“He prophesieth of the times that are far off” — conceding the word while escaping its claim."

"“He that prophesieth edifieth the church” — the New Testament measure."
